metadata.description: Trading Game knowledge graph definition. Both Unity and the .NET backend consume this file.
metadata.note: Positions are in graph-space units. The visual editor will read/write these.
metadata.tiers: Tier 0: Foundations, Tier 1: First Experiences, Tier 2: Deepening, Tier 3: Strategic Thinking, Tier 4: Crisis Mastery

nodes.title: What is a Company
nodes.description: Learn what companies are and why they exist.
nodes.content: A company is a legal entity formed by people to conduct business. Companies create products or services, earn revenue, and can be owned — partially or fully — by investors through shares.

nodes.title: What is a Stock
nodes.description: Understand stocks as ownership slices of a company.
nodes.content: A stock represents a share of ownership in a company. When you buy a stock, you own a small piece of that company. If the company grows and earns more, your share becomes more valuable. If it shrinks, your share loses value.

nodes.title: Market Buy / Sell
nodes.description: Execute your first trade at the current market price.
nodes.content: A market order buys or sells a stock immediately at the best available price. You're saying 'I want this stock now, whatever the current price is.' It's the simplest and fastest way to trade.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You just executed your first trade — buying stock at the current market price.
nodes.correct_action: Market orders are the simplest way to trade. As you gain experience, you'll learn when speed matters more than price control.

nodes.title: Market Hours & Price Gaps
nodes.description: Why prices can change while the market is closed.
nodes.content: Stock exchanges have set trading hours. After the market closes, trading still happens in smaller 'after-hours' and 'pre-market' sessions. News, earnings, or global events overnight can shift prices. This means a stock that closed at $100 might open at $95 or $105 the next day — this is called a 'gap.' Your portfolio value changes even while you sleep because the market prices in new information as soon as trading resumes.
nodes.trigger_explanation: A stock you held overnight opened at a different price than yesterday's close.
nodes.correct_action: This is normal — prices gap between sessions due to after-hours trading and overnight news. Factor in overnight risk when holding positions.

nodes.title: Limit Buy / Sell
nodes.description: Set your own price instead of accepting the market's.
nodes.content: A limit order lets you specify the price you're willing to pay (or accept). A buy limit says 'only buy if the price drops to X.' A sell limit says 'only sell if the price rises to X.' The trade only happens if the market reaches your price.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've placed several market orders, always accepting whatever price the market gives you.
nodes.correct_action: Use limit orders to set the exact price you're willing to pay or accept, giving you more control over your trades.

nodes.title: Volatility
nodes.description: A stock you hold just moved sharply. Here's why.
nodes.content: Volatility measures how much a stock's price swings. High volatility means big moves up and down. Low volatility means steady prices. Volatile stocks offer bigger potential gains — but also bigger losses.
nodes.trigger_explanation: A stock you're holding just moved more than 5% in a single day.
nodes.correct_action: Expect volatility when holding individual stocks. Consider whether the position size matches your comfort with big daily swings.

nodes.title: Diversification
nodes.description: Your portfolio is concentrated. Spreading risk matters.
nodes.content: Diversification means owning multiple different stocks so that one bad performer doesn't sink your whole portfolio. If all your money is in one company and it drops 30%, your whole portfolio drops 30%. Spread across five companies, that same drop only hits 6% of your total.
nodes.trigger_explanation: Over 80% of your portfolio is in a single stock. If that company has a bad day, your whole portfolio takes the hit.
nodes.correct_action: Spread your investments across multiple stocks so one bad performer doesn't sink everything.

nodes.title: Locking in Gains
nodes.description: You just made your first profitable trade.
nodes.content: Congratulations — you sold for more than you paid. That's a realized gain. Until you sell, any profit is just 'on paper.' The discipline of knowing when to take profits is one of the hardest parts of trading.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You sold a stock for more than you paid — your first realized profit.
nodes.correct_action: Nice work. Now the question becomes: when do you take profits versus holding for more? Develop a plan for when to sell winners.

nodes.title: Taking a Loss
nodes.description: You sold for less than you paid. Every trader does.
nodes.content: You just realized a loss. This is normal — even the best traders lose on individual trades. What matters is that your wins outweigh your losses over time. The key skill is cutting losses quickly rather than hoping a bad position recovers.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You sold a stock for less than you paid — your first realized loss.
nodes.correct_action: Losses are part of trading. The key is cutting them early instead of hoping a bad position recovers. Set a mental stop-loss before you buy.

nodes.title: Cost Basis
nodes.description: You bought the same stock at different prices.
nodes.content: When you buy the same stock multiple times, your average cost basis is the weighted average of all your purchase prices. This number determines whether you're 'up' or 'down' on the position. FIFO (first in, first out) means your oldest shares are sold first.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You bought the same stock more than once, at different prices.
nodes.correct_action: Track your average cost basis — it determines whether you're actually up or down on the position, not just your latest purchase price.

nodes.title: Paper Gains vs Realized Gains
nodes.description: A position is up big — but you haven't sold yet.
nodes.content: An unrealized gain means your stock is worth more than you paid, but you haven't sold. It's 'paper profit' — it can disappear if the price drops. A realized gain is locked in when you sell. The question is always: hold for more, or take the guaranteed profit?
nodes.trigger_explanation: One of your positions is up over 20%, but you haven't sold yet — that's paper profit, not real profit.
nodes.correct_action: Decide whether to lock in your gains or hold for more. Paper profits can vanish. Consider selling part of the position to secure some profit.

nodes.title: Buying the Dip
nodes.description: You bought a stock after a significant drop.
nodes.content: Buying the dip means purchasing a stock after its price has fallen, betting it will recover. This can be smart if the company's fundamentals haven't changed — you're getting the same business at a discount. But it's risky if the price is falling for good reason.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You bought a stock after it dropped over 5% recently — that's called 'buying the dip.'
nodes.correct_action: Before buying a dip, ask why the price fell. If the company is still strong, it could be a bargain. If something fundamental changed, you might be catching a falling knife.

nodes.title: Cash Reserves
nodes.description: You're almost fully invested. Flexibility matters.
nodes.content: Keeping some cash in reserve means you can buy opportunities when they appear — a stock drops to a great price, or a market crash creates bargains. If you're 100% invested, you can only buy more by selling something else, possibly at a bad time.
nodes.trigger_explanation: Your cash reserves dropped below 10% of your total portfolio. You're almost fully invested with little flexibility.
nodes.correct_action: Keep some cash on hand so you can act on opportunities. Being 100% invested means you can only buy by selling something else, possibly at a bad time.

nodes.title: Market Downturns
nodes.description: The whole market just dropped. Here's what happened.
nodes.content: A broad market decline means most stocks are falling together. This often happens due to economic fears, interest rate changes, or unexpected events. Individual stock quality matters less during a crash — even good companies get dragged down. Historically, markets always recover, but timing the bottom is nearly impossible.
nodes.trigger_explanation: The overall market just dropped significantly — most stocks fell together.
nodes.correct_action: Don't panic sell during a broad market decline. Historically, markets recover. Focus on whether your individual holdings are still fundamentally sound.

nodes.title: Trading Phases
nodes.description: You've traded in multiple phases of the market day.
nodes.content: Pre-market and day orders execute at today's opening price — the price the market starts at each morning. Post-market orders execute at today's closing price — you've seen how the day played out. The tradeoff: acting early means committing before you know how the day ends, while waiting gives you more information but you can't undo what already happened.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've traded in different phases of the market day — experiencing both open and close pricing.
nodes.correct_action: Pay attention to when you place orders. Pre-market and day orders use the opening price; post-market orders use the close. Each has tradeoffs — information vs. speed.

nodes.title: Risk and Reward
nodes.description: You've won and lost. Now understand the tradeoff.
nodes.content: Every trade has two sides: how much you could gain, and how much you could lose. Professional traders think in terms of risk-reward ratios — risking $1 to potentially make $3 is different from risking $3 to make $1, even if the total amount is the same. Before entering any trade, ask: 'How much am I willing to lose, and is the potential gain worth that risk?'
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've made several trades now — some winners, some losers. Time to think about the pattern.
nodes.correct_action: Before every trade, define your risk: 'I'll sell if it drops X%.' Then ask if the potential upside justifies that risk.

nodes.title: Setting Exit Points
nodes.description: A position is deep in the red. When do you cut?
nodes.content: A position you hold is down significantly. Professional traders set 'stop-loss' levels before they enter a trade — a price at which they'll sell, no questions asked. Without a predetermined exit plan, it's easy to hold losing positions hoping they recover, watching small losses become large ones. The best time to decide when to sell is before you buy.
nodes.trigger_explanation: One of your positions is down over 15%. You're holding a significant unrealized loss.
nodes.correct_action: Set exit rules before you enter trades. 'If this drops X%, I sell.' Having a plan prevents small losses from becoming catastrophic ones.

nodes.title: Averaging Down
nodes.description: You keep buying the same stock. Strategy or denial?
nodes.content: You've bought the same stock multiple times as it fell. This is called 'averaging down' — lowering your cost basis by buying more at cheaper prices. It can be brilliant if the company is sound and temporarily undervalued. But if the stock is falling for good reason, you're just throwing good money after bad. Ask yourself: 'Would I buy this stock today if I didn't already own it?'
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've bought the same stock three or more times — your cost basis keeps shifting.
nodes.correct_action: Ask: 'Would I buy this stock today if I didn't already own it?' If not, you may be averaging down out of denial, not conviction.

nodes.title: Position Sizing
nodes.description: How much you allocate matters as much as what you buy.
nodes.content: How much you put into each trade matters as much as what you buy. Even a great stock can hurt your portfolio if you put too much in it. A common rule: no single position should be large enough that a bad day in that stock ruins your week. Sizing your positions relative to your total portfolio is the foundation of risk management.
nodes.trigger_explanation: Over half your portfolio is in a single stock. Even moderate concentration carries outsized risk.
nodes.correct_action: Size each position so that no single stock can make or break your portfolio. Think in percentages, not dollar amounts.

nodes.title: Extreme Volatility
nodes.description: A 10%+ daily swing. Welcome to crisis markets.
nodes.content: A stock you hold just moved more than 10% in a single day. This kind of extreme volatility is rare in normal markets but becomes common during crises. In September 2008, daily swings of 5-10% became routine. Extreme volatility often signals that the market is uncertain about something fundamental — and that prices could swing equally hard in either direction.
nodes.trigger_explanation: A stock you hold just moved over 10% in a single day — extreme volatility.
nodes.correct_action: Extreme moves signal deep uncertainty. Consider reducing position size in highly volatile stocks, or accept the risk with eyes open.

nodes.title: Correlation in a Crisis
nodes.description: Everything is falling together. Diversification has limits.
nodes.content: During calm markets, different stocks move independently — one goes up while another goes down. But in a crisis, correlations spike. Stocks that normally have nothing in common suddenly fall together. This is why diversification provides less protection in a crash than in normal times. The 2008 crisis showed that in true panic, almost everything drops.
nodes.trigger_explanation: The market just dropped severely — even your diversified holdings fell together.
nodes.correct_action: In a severe crash, diversification dampens losses but doesn't prevent them. The real protection is position sizing and cash reserves.

nodes.title: Emotional Discipline
nodes.description: Fear and greed: the two forces that move markets.
nodes.content: You've experienced gains and losses. You've watched profits evaporate and recoveries you didn't expect. The pattern behind most trading mistakes is emotional: selling in fear at the bottom, buying in greed at the top. The traders who survive long-term are the ones who develop rules and follow them — especially when every instinct says not to.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've made enough trades to have felt the pull of fear and greed. Time to build a framework.
nodes.correct_action: Write down your trading rules. Follow them mechanically. The best trades often feel uncomfortable; the worst trades often feel exciting.

nodes.title: Market Cycles
nodes.description: Bull runs end. Bear markets end. The cycle repeats.
nodes.content: Markets move in cycles. Bull markets can last years, making everyone feel like a genius. Then the cycle turns — bear markets destroy gains and test conviction. The 2007-2009 period you're living through is a complete cycle: exuberance, denial, panic, and eventually, recovery. Recognizing where you are in the cycle is more valuable than picking the right stock.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've traded through market ups and downs — you're ready to see the bigger pattern.
nodes.correct_action: Ask yourself: where are we in the cycle right now? Exuberance? Denial? Panic? Your answer should shape how aggressively you trade.

nodes.title: Cutting Losses
nodes.description: The hardest skill: admitting you were wrong.
nodes.content: Cutting a losing position is the hardest skill in trading. Your brain treats selling at a loss as 'making the loss real' — but the loss was already real the moment the price dropped. What you're actually doing is freeing up capital for better opportunities. The question isn't 'will this stock recover?' — it's 'is my money better deployed elsewhere right now?'
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've learned about stop-losses and risk-reward. Now apply them: every dollar in a losing position is a dollar not in a winning one.
nodes.correct_action: When you're holding a loser, reframe the question. Don't ask 'will it come back?' Ask 'if I had this cash right now, would I buy this stock at this price?' If not, sell.

nodes.title: Contrarian Thinking
nodes.description: Buying when everyone else is selling.
nodes.content: You just bought a stock after a steep, prolonged decline. Most investors sell in fear during downturns. Contrarians do the opposite — they buy when others panic, betting that the fear is overdone. Warren Buffett's advice: 'Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.' But contrarian thinking only works if the fundamentals support recovery. Buying a falling stock without analysis isn't contrarian — it's gambling.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You bought into a steep, sustained decline — a deeper dip than a casual pullback.
nodes.correct_action: Contrarian bets require conviction backed by analysis. Ask: is the market overreacting, or is this decline justified by fundamentals?

nodes.title: Surviving the Crisis
nodes.description: 2008 is here. Everything you've learned is being tested.
nodes.content: This is 2008. Markets are in freefall, portfolios are bleeding, and every headline is worse than the last. Everything you've learned — diversification, position sizing, emotional discipline — is being tested at once. The students of history know that markets have always recovered from crashes. The question is: can you stay solvent and rational long enough to benefit from that recovery?
nodes.trigger_explanation: The market is in freefall. This is the crisis. Everything you've built is being tested.
nodes.correct_action: Survive. Don't panic sell everything. Preserve capital. Look for the strongest companies at crisis prices. The recovery will come — be positioned to benefit.

nodes.title: Hindsight and Foresight
nodes.description: You've lived through the crisis. What patterns will you recognize next time?
nodes.content: You've traded through the 2007-2009 financial crisis. You've felt the overconfidence of a bull market, the denial as cracks appeared, and the panic when everything collapsed. These patterns repeat — different triggers, same human psychology. The housing crisis of 2008, the dot-com crash of 2000, the 1987 Black Monday — each followed the same emotional arc. What you've built isn't just trading skill. It's pattern recognition for the next crisis.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You've traded through the full crisis cycle. Time to see the big picture.
nodes.correct_action: The patterns you've learned — euphoria, denial, panic, recovery — will repeat in your lifetime. The next crisis will feel different but follow the same emotional arc. You'll be ready.

nodes.title: What is a Market
nodes.description: Understand where stocks are traded and how prices form.
nodes.content: A stock market is a place where buyers and sellers meet to trade shares of companies. Prices aren't set by anyone — they emerge from supply and demand. When more people want to buy a stock than sell it, the price rises. When more want to sell, it drops. Stock exchanges like the NYSE and NASDAQ provide the infrastructure, rules, and transparency that make this possible.

nodes.title: Crashes Through History
nodes.description: Markets have crashed before. They will again.
nodes.content: Market crashes aren't rare — they're structural. The 1929 crash triggered the Great Depression. Black Monday in 1987 saw the Dow drop 22% in a single day. The dot-com bubble burst in 2000 when internet stocks collapsed. Each time, the pattern repeated: euphoria, overvaluation, a trigger, panic, and eventually recovery. The specifics change. The human psychology doesn't.

nodes.title: The Housing Boom
nodes.description: The setup for 2008: easy credit and the belief that housing never falls.
nodes.content: Between 2003 and 2006, U.S. housing prices soared. Interest rates were low, mortgages were easy to get, and everyone believed housing was a safe investment. Banks packaged thousands of mortgages into complex financial products and sold them worldwide. The assumption underpinning everything: housing prices only go up. When that assumption broke, so did the financial system.

nodes.title: The Subprime Crisis
nodes.description: The market is dropping. Here's what's happening behind the headlines.
nodes.content: Subprime mortgages were loans given to borrowers who couldn't really afford them. Banks bundled these risky loans into securities (CDOs) and sold them as 'safe' investments. When homeowners started defaulting, the value of these securities collapsed — and so did the banks holding them. What started as a housing problem became a banking crisis, then a stock market crash. The complexity of the financial products meant nobody knew who was holding the bad debt.
nodes.trigger_explanation: The market just dropped. Behind the numbers, the subprime mortgage crisis is unfolding.
nodes.correct_action: Pay attention to what's driving the decline. When the cause is systemic — not just one company — the effects ripple through everything.

nodes.title: Contagion
nodes.description: Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers. When one domino falls, they all do.
nodes.content: In March 2008, Bear Stearns collapsed and was acquired in an emergency deal. Six months later, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest in American history. The failure of these institutions triggered panic across the global financial system. Banks stopped lending to each other. Credit markets froze. The stock market went into freefall. A housing problem had become a global financial crisis because the system was interconnected in ways nobody fully understood.
nodes.trigger_explanation: Major financial institutions are failing. The crisis is spreading.
nodes.correct_action: In a contagion, even strong companies fall because the financial system itself is under stress. Focus on preserving capital, not finding bargains — yet.

nodes.title: Government Response
nodes.description: TARP, bailouts, and rate cuts. When governments step in.
nodes.content: As the crisis deepened, governments intervened on an unprecedented scale. The U.S. passed the $700 billion TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program) to buy toxic assets from banks. The Federal Reserve cut interest rates to near zero and began 'quantitative easing' — essentially creating money to buy bonds and stabilize markets. The question that still divides economists: was bailing out the banks necessary to prevent total collapse, or did it reward reckless behavior and set the stage for the next crisis?
nodes.trigger_explanation: The crisis has forced government intervention. Markets are in uncharted territory.
nodes.correct_action: Government intervention can stabilize markets, but it takes time. The bottom often comes when fear is at its peak — not when the news gets better.

nodes.title: Anatomy of a Recovery
nodes.description: March 2009: the bottom nobody recognized at the time.
nodes.content: On March 9, 2009, the S&P 500 hit its crisis low of 676 — down 57% from its peak. At the time, headlines were apocalyptic. Nobody rang a bell at the bottom. The recovery started quietly, driven by investors who bought when fear was at its maximum. Within a year, the market had recovered over 60%. Within five years, it had set new highs. The lesson: the best time to invest is often when it feels the worst. But recognizing the bottom in real time is nearly impossible.
nodes.trigger_explanation: You bought into a severe decline. In March 2009, the bravest investors did exactly this.
nodes.correct_action: You can't time the exact bottom. But buying quality assets during maximum fear, with money you don't need immediately, has historically been rewarded.
